text: Performance Troubleshooting taught the Slow Request Log and the Script Performance Profiler — real tools for when a form or a script is already slow. That entire course is reactive by design: something has already degraded, and the job is finding out why. A Technical Architect's job starts earlier. This lesson is about the decisions made before a table, an integration, or a line of script ever reaches production — decisions that leave the Slow Request Log far less to find.

Reactive diagnosis fixes a problem that already exists. Proactive architecture prevents a whole class of those problems from happening at all — by deciding table design before launch, sizing an integration pattern to real anticipated volume, and catching performance anti-patterns in code review before they ever merge into production.

Chapter 3's table design lesson covered choosing extension versus composition, and indexing the fields that will actually carry query load, before the table ever goes live. Retrofitting an index after a list view has been timing out for months means a schema change against live production data, a resource-consuming re-index, and users who already felt the slowdown. Deciding it upfront means that slowdown never happens.

Chapter 4's event-driven-versus-request-response lesson made the tradeoff explicit: a synchronous integration that works fine at fifty transactions a day can become the platform's primary bottleneck at five thousand, because every request holds a semaphore for the call's duration. Choosing the pattern against real volume projections, at design time, is the proactive version of a decision Performance Troubleshooting's semaphore lesson would otherwise have to diagnose.

GlideRecord Performance Pitfalls and Common Business Rule Mistakes teach developers to recognize unbounded queries inside a loop, recursive Business Rule triggers, and filters that drive a full table scan. A code review standard that explicitly checks for those same anti-patterns catches them before they reach a customer-facing instance. The architect's leverage is mandating that standard exists and is enforced — not personally catching every mistake by hand.
Table design, integration pattern, and code review standards: three decisions made before launch, not after a diagnosis. Next up: capacity planning for a growing instance.
